Edge-weight stability and split-half reliability

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/network-reliability.Rmd
network-reliability.Rmd

A psychological network is estimated from one sample, and another sample from the same population would give a somewhat different network. Before an edge is interpreted or a node is called the most central, the analyst needs to know whether the result would reappear: whether an edge differs reliably from zero, whether two nodes can be ranked, and whether the structure survives when part of the sample is removed or when the sample is split in two. Resampling answers these questions without distributional assumptions, by re-estimating the network many times on samples drawn from the data (Epskamp et al., 2018).

This article applies five such diagnostics to one network: bootstrap confidence intervals for edges and centralities, bootstrap tests of differences between nodes, the stability of centrality and of edge weights when cases are dropped, and the agreement of networks estimated on two halves of the sample. Each diagnostic refits the network with the same estimator, so the same steps apply to any estimator.

library(psychnets)
set.seed(1)

The diagnostics resample at random, so the seed is set once to make the results reproducible.

Data

SRL_Claude holds 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire generated by a large language model (Claude) in a study of how such models answer psychological surveys (Saqr, 2025). Its responses are more internally consistent than human responses, which yields a network with large edges; it serves here as an example and is not evidence about students.

  • Nodes: five construct scores on a scale from 1 to 7: CSU (cognitive strategy use), IV (intrinsic value), SE (self-efficacy), SR (self-regulation) and TA (test anxiety).
  • Observations: one row per respondent; the data are complete.
head(SRL_Claude)
#>        CSU       IV       SE       SR   TA
#> 1 4.615385 6.444444 4.555556 4.777778 4.00
#> 2 5.692308 7.000000 5.555556 6.222222 3.00
#> 3 5.692308 7.000000 5.777778 6.666667 3.75
#> 4 5.461538 6.222222 5.777778 5.777778 4.75
#> 5 4.846154 5.333333 5.000000 5.333333 3.75
#> 6 4.538462 4.333333 5.777778 4.000000 5.00

Every diagnostic below estimates an EBIC graphical lasso (method = "glasso"), whose edges are partial correlations.

How precise is each edge?

net_boot() draws bootstrap samples of the respondents with replacement, re-estimates the network on each, and summarizes the distribution of every edge weight: its mean, its 95% percentile interval, and the proportion of samples in which the edge was selected. An edge is flagged significant when its interval excludes zero. An applied analysis uses at least 1,000 samples; 200 keep this example short.

b <- net_boot(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", n_boot = 200, cores = 1)
b
#> <psychnet_bootstrap> glasso, 200 resamples, 95% CI
#>   10 edges (8 significant), 5 nodes, measures: strength, expected_influence
as.data.frame(b)
#>    from to     observed        mean      lower      upper prop_nonzero
#> 1   CSU IV  0.001744267  0.02777141  0.0000000  0.1202986        0.550
#> 2   CSU SE  0.223973564  0.22825629  0.1360369  0.3243276        1.000
#> 3    IV SE -0.402239002 -0.40747351 -0.5171210 -0.2997294        1.000
#> 4   CSU SR  0.728177591  0.72069631  0.6520409  0.7748107        1.000
#> 5    IV SR  0.574170376  0.55984489  0.4974457  0.6284297        1.000
#> 6    SE SR  0.221496430  0.22481115  0.1522627  0.3150743        1.000
#> 7   CSU TA  0.525584044  0.52512504  0.4465139  0.6111719        1.000
#> 8    IV TA -0.013854928 -0.03375546 -0.1320652  0.0245725        0.755
#> 9    SE TA -0.417575459 -0.41986895 -0.4934429 -0.3408875        1.000
#> 10   SR TA -0.428181457 -0.42032870 -0.4852677 -0.3476119        1.000
#>    significant
#> 1        FALSE
#> 2         TRUE
#> 3         TRUE
#> 4         TRUE
#> 5         TRUE
#> 6         TRUE
#> 7         TRUE
#> 8        FALSE
#> 9         TRUE
#> 10        TRUE

Eight of the ten edges have intervals that exclude zero and are selected in every bootstrap sample. The strongest, CSU–SR (0.73, interval 0.65 to 0.77), is estimated precisely. Two edges are not reliable. CSU–IV has an observed weight of 0.002 and an interval from 0 to 0.12, and is selected in only 55% of the samples; IV–TA (-0.014, interval -0.13 to 0.02) is selected in 76%. Neither their presence nor their sign can be interpreted at this sample size. The plot shows each edge with its interval, ordered by size:

plot(b)

How precise is each node’s centrality?

The same bootstrap samples give intervals for the centrality of each node.

as.data.frame(b, what = "centrality")
#>   node  strength strength_lower strength_upper expected_influence
#> 1  CSU 1.4794795      1.3523996       1.667857          1.4794795
#> 2   IV 0.9920086      0.8349704       1.266730          0.1598207
#> 3   SE 1.2652845      1.0903270       1.502809         -0.3743445
#> 4   SR 1.9520259      1.8288036       2.030832          1.0956629
#> 5   TA 1.3851959      1.2491191       1.574835         -0.3340278
#>   expected_influence_lower expected_influence_upper
#> 1               1.35239959                1.6678566
#> 2               0.01245256                0.2507549
#> 3              -0.45804609               -0.2573138
#> 4               0.96124498                1.2166942
#> 5              -0.43162878               -0.2568683
plot(b, type = "centrality")

Self-regulation has the largest strength, 1.95 with an interval from 1.83 to 2.03, which does not overlap with the interval of any other node. Intrinsic value has the smallest strength (0.99, interval 0.83 to 1.27). The intervals of cognitive strategy use, self-efficacy and test anxiety overlap, so their order cannot be read from the intervals alone; the difference test below addresses it. Expected influence separates the nodes differently, because self-efficacy and test anxiety have negative expected influence (-0.37 and -0.33).

Which nodes can be ranked?

difference_test() tests whether two nodes differ in centrality, or two edges in weight, within the network. For each pair it takes the difference in every bootstrap sample, forms its percentile interval and a two-sided bootstrap p-value, and flags the pair when the interval excludes zero. It reads the samples already stored by net_boot(), so nothing is refitted. With ten pairs, p_adjust = "BH" controls the false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

difference_test(b, type = "strength", p_adjust = "BH")
#>    item1 item2    value1    value2    obs_diff        lower       upper
#> 1    CSU    IV 1.4794795 0.9920086  0.48747089  0.241546367  0.66372411
#> 2    CSU    SE 1.4794795 1.2652845  0.21419501  0.038286544  0.42634973
#> 3     IV    SE 0.9920086 1.2652845 -0.27327588 -0.334413124 -0.13532664
#> 4    CSU    SR 1.4794795 1.9520259 -0.47254639 -0.623609013 -0.21321640
#> 5     IV    SR 0.9920086 1.9520259 -0.96001728 -1.093928157 -0.59055176
#> 6     SE    SR 1.2652845 1.9520259 -0.68674140 -0.877109385 -0.38029431
#> 7    CSU    TA 1.4794795 1.3851959  0.09428358  0.003900685  0.19887099
#> 8     IV    TA 0.9920086 1.3851959 -0.39318731 -0.563676398 -0.15302913
#> 9     SE    TA 1.2652845 1.3851959 -0.11991143 -0.332646886  0.08003091
#> 10    SR    TA 1.9520259 1.3851959  0.56682997  0.285722615  0.69319578
#>       p_value significant
#> 1  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 2  0.04444444        TRUE
#> 3  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 4  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 5  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 6  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 7  0.04444444        TRUE
#> 8  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 9  0.26000000       FALSE
#> 10 0.00000000        TRUE

Nine of the ten pairs differ. Self-regulation is stronger than every other node (all adjusted p < 0.01), and cognitive strategy use is stronger than self-efficacy and test anxiety (adjusted p = 0.044 for both). The one pair that cannot be ordered is self-efficacy and test anxiety: their difference is -0.12, with an interval from -0.33 to 0.08 and p = 0.26. A report can rank self-regulation first and intrinsic value last, but should not order self-efficacy and test anxiety.

Is the centrality ranking stable when cases are dropped?

net_stability() re-estimates the network on random subsets that drop an increasing proportion of the respondents and correlates the centralities of each subset with those of the full sample. The correlation-stability coefficient (CS-coefficient) is the largest proportion of cases that can be dropped while the correlation stays at or above 0.7 in at least 95% of the subsets (Epskamp et al., 2018).

st <- net_stability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
st
#> <psychnet_stability> glasso, 100 subsets/proportion
#>   CS-coefficient (pearson cor > 0.70 in > 95% of subsets):
#>     strength             0.70
#>     expected_influence   0.90

The CS-coefficient is 0.70 for strength and 0.90 for expected influence. Up to 70% of the respondents can be dropped and the strength values of the subsets still correlate at least 0.7 with those of the full sample in 95% of the subsets. Epskamp et al. (2018) suggest a CS-coefficient of at least 0.25, and preferably 0.5, before centrality is interpreted; both measures exceed it, so the centrality order of this network can be reported. The plot shows the mean correlation at each drop proportion with a band of one standard deviation and the 0.7 threshold:

plot(st)

Is the edge structure stable when cases are dropped?

net_casedrop_reliability() applies the same case-dropping design to the edges. At each drop proportion it compares the edge weights of each subset with those of the full sample through their correlation and through the mean, median and largest absolute difference. The edge-weight CS-coefficient is defined as for centrality.

cd <- net_casedrop_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
cd
#> # edge-weight stability: glasso | CS = 0.90 (pearson cor > 0.70 in > 95% of subsets)

The edge-weight CS-coefficient is 0.90. The correlation between subset and full-sample edges is 0.999 when 10% of the cases are dropped and still 0.943 when 90% are dropped, so the pattern of edges is preserved even in small subsets. The absolute differences show the cost in precision: the mean difference grows from 0.012 at a 10% drop to 0.112 at a 90% drop, and the largest single-edge difference from 0.028 to 0.261. The pattern is stable, but individual edge values estimated from a small subsample can be off by more than 0.2.

plot(cd)

Does the network replicate across halves of the sample?

net_split_reliability() divides the sample at random into two halves, estimates a network on each, and compares the two sets of edges, repeating the split many times. The result has one row per comparison measure, with its mean, standard deviation and the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles across splits.

rel <- net_split_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
rel
#> # split-half reliability: glasso | 100 iterations (50/50 split)
#>           metric       mean         sd      lower     upper n_valid
#> 1   mean_abs_dev 0.06406132 0.02201012 0.03319670 0.1092927     100
#> 2 median_abs_dev 0.05674286 0.02297601 0.02204948 0.1086049     100
#> 3    correlation 0.98243129 0.01208858 0.95313106 0.9960735     100
#> 4    max_abs_dev 0.14177087 0.05219793 0.06749545 0.2635560     100

Across 100 splits, the edges of the two halves correlate 0.982 on average, with 95% of the splits between 0.953 and 0.996. Two independent samples of 150 respondents thus recover nearly the same edge structure. The mean absolute difference between the halves is 0.064, and the largest single-edge difference averages 0.142: a typical edge moves by less than 0.1 between halves, while the least stable edge can move by about 0.14.

plot(rel)

Do the diagnostics apply to other estimators?

Each diagnostic refits the network through psychnet(method = ), so it applies to any estimator. With the unregularized partial correlation network:

net_casedrop_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "pcor", iter = 100)
#> # edge-weight stability: pcor | CS = 0.90 (pearson cor > 0.70 in > 95% of subsets)

The partial correlation network has the same edge-weight CS-coefficient (0.90), with slightly larger differences than the graphical lasso at every drop proportion (mean absolute difference 0.139 against 0.112 at a 90% drop), because no penalty stabilizes the small edges. Each diagnostic also accepts a set of group networks built with psychnet(..., group = ) and returns one result per group.

When to use which diagnostic

Question Verb Read the result with
How precise is each edge and centrality? net_boot() as.data.frame(b), as.data.frame(b, what = "centrality"), plot()
Do two edges or two nodes differ? difference_test() the returned table, plot()
Is the centrality order stable when cases are dropped? net_stability() as.data.frame(st, what = "cs"), as.data.frame(st), plot()
Is the edge structure stable when cases are dropped? net_casedrop_reliability() the returned table, plot()
Does the network replicate across halves? net_split_reliability() the returned table, plot()
  • Report bootstrap intervals with every edge that is interpreted, and do not interpret edges whose interval includes zero.
  • Rank nodes only after the difference test and the CS-coefficient support the ranking; a CS-coefficient below 0.25 means that centrality should not be interpreted.
  • Case-dropping and split-half reliability describe the whole structure; bootstrap intervals describe individual edges. A network can be stable as a whole while some of its edges are not, as in this example.
  • All diagnostics assume that the respondents are independent. Repeated measures of the same persons need a resampling scheme that keeps each person’s observations together.

References

Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate: A practical and powerful approach to multiple testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 57(1), 289-300. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x

Epskamp, S., Borsboom, D., & Fried, E. I. (2018). Estimating psychological networks and their accuracy: A tutorial paper. Behavior Research Methods, 50(1), 195-212. doi:10.3758/s13428-017-0862-1

Saqr, M. (2025). Delving into the psychology of machines: Exploring the structure of self-regulated learning via LLM-generated survey responses. Computers in Human Behavior, 173, 108769. doi:10.1016/j.chb.2025.108769
